prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse near-to-far layout: a person occupies the near left-to-centre foreground about 0.4–1.0 m from the camera, while the counter, pans, bowls, and bottles extend behind and to the person’s right at roughly 0.7–2 m; the person’s arms and the camera wearer’s visible hand are among the nearest surfaces. Across the five frames, the person shifts from left toward centre, turns slightly, and extends an arm toward a cup or container on the right, while the camera wearer’s hand moves from the left edge to the centre-right foreground; the major background surfaces remain farther and relatively fixed. Brightness boundaries reveal that the outstretched hands and held container are in front of the torso and that the torso occludes much of the rear counter, distinctions that are less obvious amid the RGB texture. Metric distances are only rough because the map has no scale, compresses many background objects into similar gray levels, loses detail at dark boundaries, and appears inconsistent around the person’s hair, arms, and the frame edges.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates a nearby person from several countertop objects: bowls lie mainly in front of and to the right of the person, bottles stand farther back along the upper-right background, and a cup appears near the person’s extended hand in frame 4; most are approximately 0.5–1.5 m from the camera and within about 0.2–0.8 m of the person’s hands. Across frames the person mask moves from the left edge toward the centre and changes outline as the body turns and the right arm reaches across the scene, while bowl and bottle masks shift laterally with the egocentric camera motion. The masks make object separation, overlap, and partial visibility clearer than RGB—for example, the person occludes parts of the work surface, several bottles are only small upper-edge regions, and bowls remain distinct where their colors and contents blend into the counter. The map is unreliable where labels flicker or are implausible: the large counter region is called an oven, one upper region is called a cat, a hand-held item alternates among cup, bottle, and person, and several visible utensils, pans, and vegetables are missing or only partly masked.
descriptions.pose: The pose map primarily supports limb geometry rather than full scene layout: magenta hand skeletons place the camera wearer’s hand in the near left foreground in frame 1 and near the centre-right in later frames, while frame 5 adds a yellow arm segment extending from the upper-left toward a hand near the centre-right. The hand positions track a left-to-right movement and changing wrist orientation across the five frames, with the most articulated hand about 0.3–0.7 m from the camera and apparently within arm’s reach; in the final frame the yellow forearm and magenta hand show a continuous reach direction. The skeletons expose finger spread, wrist orientation, and the connection between forearm and hand more clearly than the RGB, especially where hands overlap similarly colored clothing or objects. The map is incomplete and unreliable for broader spatial judgments: most body joints, heads, gaze directions, and the other person’s posture are absent, isolated hand skeletons are not consistently attributable to a particular person, and truncation or occlusion near frame edges prevents determining who faces or looks toward the camera.
